title: 14.12–14.14 Blood, Blood Vessels & Circulatory System Types
subtitle: Plasma, RBC/WBC/Platelets, Table 14.1 Arteries vs Veins vs Capillaries, and Open vs Closed circulation (pp. 204–207)
curiosity_hook: Why do arteries have thick elastic walls without internal valves, while veins have thin walls WITH valves — and why do mature human RBCs discard their own nucleus?
source_verified_by: AGY Pass 2 Full-Chapter Build (pending human biology teacher sign-off)
learning_objectives: Explain the roles of blood plasma (55%) and formed elements — biconcave enucleated RBCs (120-day lifespan), WBCs (granulocytes & agranulocytes), and platelets (clotting).
Contrast Arteries, Veins, and single-cell-thick Capillaries (~8 µm) using Table 14.1 criteria including the pulmonary artery/vein exceptions.
Differentiate Open circulatory systems (haemocoel sinuses in Arthropods/Molluscs) from Closed circulatory systems discovered by William Harvey (1628).

concept_outline.heading: Composition of Blood (14.12, pp. 204–206)
concept_outline.summary: Blood consists of 55% slightly alkaline plasma plus RBCs (erythrocytes: haemoglobin, no nucleus/mitochondria/ER so maximum O₂ capacity & capillary flexibility, lifespan 120 days), WBCs (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, lymphocytes producing antibodies, phagocytic monocytes), and platelets (thrombocytes: 2.5–4 lakh/mm³, clotting).

concept_outline.heading: Arteries, Veins & Capillaries (14.13, Table 14.1, p. 206)
concept_outline.summary: Arteries distribute high-pressure blood away from the heart through thick elastic deep walls without internal valves (all oxygenated EXCEPT pulmonary artery). Veins collect low-pressure blood back to the heart through thin superficial walls WITH internal valves (all deoxygenated EXCEPT pulmonary vein). Capillaries (~8 µm, single endothelial layer) exchange gases and nutrients.

concept_outline.heading: Open vs Closed Circulatory Systems (14.14, p. 207)
concept_outline.summary: In Open systems (arthropods, molluscs, ascidians), blood enters open body cavities (haemocoel sinuses) without capillaries. In Closed systems (vertebrates, discovered by William Harvey in 1628), blood stays inside a closed circuit of arteries → capillaries → veins.

key_terms.definition: Biconcave, enucleated red blood cells containing haemoglobin for O₂ transport (lifespan ~120 days).
Small enucleated fragments (lifespan 8–10 days) essential for blood clotting at injury sites.
Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood (RV → lungs); Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood (lungs → LA).
Father of Modern Physiology who discovered the closed human blood circulatory system.

steps.heading: Blood = 55% Plasma + Formed Elements
steps.description: RBCs carry O₂, WBCs defend via phagocytosis & antibodies, Platelets clot wounds.
steps.key_takeaway: Anaemia = low RBC; Thrombocytopenia = low platelets.

steps.heading: Arteries vs Veins vs Capillaries
steps.description: Arteries = thick, high pressure, no valves; Veins = thin, low pressure, valves present; Capillaries = 8 µm single-cell exchange tubes.
steps.key_takeaway: Remember the pulmonary artery & pulmonary vein oxygen exceptions.

steps.heading: Open vs Closed Circulation
steps.description: Open = haemocoel sinuses (insects/molluscs); Closed = continuous vessels + capillaries (vertebrates).
steps.key_takeaway: Closed circulation was discovered by William Harvey (1628).

question_bank.prompt: Why does a mature mammalian Red Blood Corpuscle (RBC) lack mitochondria (p. 205)?
question_bank.hint: Think about what mitochondria consume during aerobic respiration.

options.label: So the RBC does not consume oxygen itself and can deliver ALL its oxygen to tissues
options.feedback: Correct! Lack of mitochondria preserves oxygen for delivery; lack of nucleus makes it biconcave; lack of ER boosts capillary flexibility.

options.label: So it can produce antibodies faster
options.feedback: Lymphocytes (a type of WBC) produce antibodies, not RBCs.

options.label: So it can live for 10 years

question_bank.worked_explanation: Textbook p. 205 highlights all three adaptations: no nucleus (biconcave O₂ surface area), no mitochondria (saves O₂ for tissues), no ER (flexibility in narrow capillaries).

question_bank.prompt: Which blood vessel is the ONLY vein in the human body that carries OXYGENATED blood (Table 14.1, p. 206)?
question_bank.hint: It returns freshly oxygenated blood from the lungs to the Left Atrium.

options.label: Superior Vena Cava
options.feedback: Vena cava carries deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.

options.label: Pulmonary Vein
options.feedback: Correct! Pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood from lungs to the left atrium.

options.label: Pulmonary Artery
options.feedback: Pulmonary artery is an artery carrying deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

options.label: Coronary Sinus
options.feedback: Coronary sinus drains deoxygenated blood from cardiac muscle into the right atrium.

question_bank.worked_explanation: All veins carry deoxygenated blood EXCEPT pulmonary veins; all arteries carry oxygenated blood EXCEPT pulmonary arteries.

question_bank.prompt: Who discovered the closed circulatory system in 1628 and is called the Father of Modern Physiology (p. 207)?
question_bank.hint: Check the 'More to Know' box on p. 207.

options.label: Karl Landsteiner
options.feedback: Landsteiner discovered ABO blood groups (1900) and Rh factor (1940).

options.label: William Harvey
options.feedback: Correct! William Harvey (1628) discovered closed blood circulation.

options.label: Wilhelm His
options.feedback: His (1893) discovered the atrioventricular Bundle of His.

options.label: Nehemiah Grew
options.feedback: Nehemiah Grew is the Father of Plant Anatomy (Unit 12).

question_bank.worked_explanation: William Harvey (1628) demonstrated closed circulation and is revered as the Father of Modern Physiology.

worked_feedback: Always pair vessel structure with blood pressure: high pressure → thick elastic artery; low pressure → thin valved vein.

flashcards.back: RBC: ~120 days (O₂ transport); WBC: immunity (neutrophils/lymphocytes/monocytes); Platelets: 8–10 days (clotting).
Artery = thick, elastic, deep, high pressure, no internal valves. Vein = thin, non-elastic, superficial, low pressure, internal valves.
Open: blood enters haemocoel sinuses (arthropods, molluscs). Closed: blood stays in vessels + capillaries (vertebrates).
